title: Barnabas Bookshop Fire
subject: Criminal Law & Procedure
stem:
Question ID: 14718_barnabas_bookshop_fire
Transformed from: 14718

Barnabas owned a small Christian bookstore in a strip mall. A large discount Bible-and-gift shop opened in a new shopping mall nearby, and Barnabas learned that he would have to close his store. In desperation, he decided to set fire to his store to collect the insurance.

While looking in the stockroom for flammable material, Barnabas lit a match to read the label on a can. The match burned his finger and, in a reflex action, he dropped it. It fell into a cardboard recycling bin and ignited some paper. Barnabas could have put out the fire, but instead left the building because he wanted the building destroyed. The fire spread, and the store was destroyed.

Barnabas was arrested and indicted for arson. Barnabas is:

choices.A: guilty, because he could have put out the fire before it spread and did not do so because he wanted the building destroyed.
choices.B: guilty, because he was negligent in starting the fire.
choices.C: not guilty, because even if he wanted to burn the building there was no concurrence between his mens rea and the act of starting the fire.
choices.D: not guilty, because his starting the fire was the result of a reflex action and not a voluntary act.

rightExplanation:
A is correct.

Gold Key: Arson is a malice crime. Negligence is too low. Specific intent to start the fire or burn the building down is not required. Reckless disregard of an obvious or high risk that the structure will burn is enough.

Silver Key: Do not freeze the act at the first spark. When the stem gives a reflex start plus a later chance to stop the fire, the later voluntary choice is the fact that matters.

Barnabas did not merely drop a match by reflex and walk into a completed accidental fire. He saw a small fire, could put it out, and chose to leave because he wanted the building destroyed. That later choice makes A the true-and-responsive answer.

wrongExplanations.B: B gives the right outcome but the wrong legal reason. Negligence alone is not enough for arson. Gold Key: arson needs malice, and malice can be supplied by reckless disregard of an obvious or high risk. B stops too low on the mental-state ladder.
wrongExplanations.C: C is the dominant trap. It sounds like a careful concurrence answer, but it frames the crime as if arson required specific intent to start the exact fire. Gold Key: arson is not a specific-intent crime. The malicious burning is enough when the defendant consciously lets the fire become destructive.
wrongExplanations.D: D is half right about the first spark. A reflex is not a voluntary act. But D answers only the first-spark question. Silver Key: once the stem gives a later voluntary choice—he could put out the fire and instead left because he wanted the building destroyed—the reflex point no longer controls.

c3.label: CUT B
c3.text: wrong mental-state level. “Negligent” is a true-sounding fact reason, but Gold Key says negligence alone is too low for arson.

c3.label: CUT C
c3.text: wrong specific-intent/concurrence frame. The answer wrongly treats arson as requiring specific intent to start the exact fire. Gold Key kills it.

c3.label: CUT D
c3.text: wrong timing / wrong element. It focuses on the reflex start and ignores the later voluntary choice to let the fire spread.

c3.label: Residual
c3.text: A. It uses the later voluntary choice plus the desire for destruction.

studentScript: I am not deciding the first spark only. B is negligence-only. C turns arson into specific intent. D stops at the reflex start. A uses the later chance to put it out and the desire for destruction. Pick A.

A.signal: Uses the later voluntary choice and the desire for destruction, not merely the reflex match drop.
A.lawyer: Arson malice can be satisfied by reckless disregard of an obvious or high risk of burning; specific intent to burn down the building is not required.

B.signal: The answer gives the guilty outcome but stops at negligence.
B.lawyer: Negligence alone is insufficient for malicious burning.

C.signal: The answer frames arson as if the mens rea must coincide with the exact act of starting the fire.
C.lawyer: Arson is a malice crime; the malicious burning does not require specific intent to start the exact fire.

D.signal: True about the reflex start, but it does not answer the later voluntary letting-burn fact.
D.lawyer: The later voluntary failure to extinguish the fire, combined with the desire for destruction, supports culpability despite the initial reflex.

goldKeys.statement: Arson is a malice crime: negligence is too low, and specific intent to start the exact fire is not required. Reckless disregard of an obvious or high risk that the structure will burn is enough.

remediation.title: Malice ladder for arson
remediation.signal: Answer array offers negligence, specific intent, reflex, and later letting-burn.
remediation.studentMove: First identify the later voluntary choice. Then apply the Gold Key: negligence no, specific-intent trap no, reckless/high-risk burning yes.
remediation.tinyRule: Arson malice sits above negligence and below specific intent.
remediation.trap: Freezing the act at the first spark.
